deep.reconstruction:
Setting, continued from the previous page. Fix a 3-element set I and, for each i in I, a 2-element set Phi_i (a mu_2-torsor). The combinatorial cube C has vertex set prod_i Phi_i. The combinatorial octahedron O has vertex set the disjoint union of the Phi_i. Both carry the antipodal involution a, which swaps the two points of every Phi_i. The quotients C~ = C/{1,a} and O~ = O/{1,a} are the 'big' (formerly 'projective') figures, i.e. the hemicube and the hemi-octahedron. O~ is the cell decomposition of RP^2 by three lines indexed by I: 3 vertices, 6 edges, 4 faces.

This page:
(i) The functors C -> C~ and O -> O~ are not faithful (hence not fully faithful). The antipodal map a is a nontrivial automorphism of C but induces the identity on C~ (and likewise for O).
(ii) Restricting to oriented cubes and oriented octahedra, with orientation-preserving isomorphisms, does give equivalences of categories, diagram (5): oriented cubes ≃ hemicubes and oriented octahedra ≃ hemi-octahedra. The vertical maps (cube <-> octahedron duality) are also equivalences. The quasi-inverse is the canonical orientation double cover: from C~ or O~ one recovers C or O, canonically oriented. At the level of groups this is the classical fact that the rotation group of the cube is S_4, which is also the full automorphism group of the hemicube and of the hemi-octahedron.
(iii) Formula (6) gives the orientation torsor intrinsically: omega(C) ≃ omega(O) ≃ (∧_{i∈I} Phi_i) ∧ or(I). Here ∧ is the contracted product of Z/2-torsors, and or(I) is the torsor of the two cyclic orders on I, i.e. the orientations of the finite set I. This is a sign-bookkeeping statement: flipping one Phi_i (a reflection) reverses orientation, and a transposition of coordinates reverses orientation. The marginal (6 bis) reformulates it: an orientation of C (or O) is the same as an isomorphism ∧Phi_i ≃ or(I).
(iv) Local structure of O~. For i in I, the line D_i is the image of the 'equator' of O orthogonal to axis i. Its two edges correspond to Phi_j × Phi_k modulo ±, that is, to the two bijections Phi_j ≃ Phi_k. Hence the edge torsor of D_i is A_i = ∧_{alpha≠i} Phi_alpha, as in (7). The two vertices on D_i form S_i ≃ I∖{i} (stated at the top of the next page). This sets up the computation on the next page: the orientation torsor of D_i viewed as a bigon is Omega_i = S_i ∧ A_i, and one finds ∧ Omega_i ≃ or(I).

Purpose: an intrinsic, torsor-level description of the simplest arrangement of three (pseudo)lines in the projective plane and its double cover. It is preparatory material for a combinatorial theory of systems of pseudo-lines.
errors: No mathematical error found. The non-faithfulness argument is correct.
The equivalence (5) is correct: the orientation double cover has a canonical orientation, and Aut^+(cube) ≅ S_4 ≅ Aut(hemicube) ≅ Aut(hemi-octahedron).
Formula (6) is consistent: a flips all three Phi_i, giving a nontrivial class, so a reverses orientation, as it must for the antipodal map of S^2.
Minor: the page does not explicitly state the morphisms of the 'oriented' categories; they must be the orientation-preserving isomorphisms for (5) to be an equivalence.

ideas.what: Hemicube and hemi-octahedron as antipodal quotients; the hemi-octahedron is the arrangement of three lines in RP^2.
ideas.modern_name: Hemi-cube / hemi-octahedron (abstract regular polyhedra; projective polyhedra)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme discusses regular maps and polyhedra generally; this specific treatment is not known there

ideas.what: Oriented cubes/octahedra are equivalent, as categories, to their projective quotients via the canonical orientation double cover; the unoriented quotient functor is not faithful.
ideas.modern_name: Orientation double cover; rotation group of the cube ≅ S_4

ideas.what: Intrinsic orientation torsor of the cube as a contracted product of Z/2-torsors: omega(C) ≃ (∧Phi_i) ∧ or(I).
ideas.modern_name: Orientation torsor / determinant line (sign) of a product of 0-spheres; Z/2-graded determinant bookkeeping
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard (determinant/orientation torsor formalism, e.g. Knudsen–Mumford style for determinants)
ideas.where_published: Torsor/contracted-product language pervades SGA; this specific formula is not known to be published

ideas.what: Edge and vertex torsors of a line in the 3-line arrangement (A_i = ∧_{alpha≠i} Phi_alpha, S_i = I∖{i}), with bigon orientation Omega_i = S_i ∧ A_i.
ideas.modern_name: Local orientation data of a pseudoline arrangement / oriented matroid chirotope of rank 3 on 3 elements
ideas.usually_credited_to: Pseudoline arrangements: Levi, Ringel, Goodman–Pollack; oriented matroids: Bland–Las Vergnas, Folkman–Lawrence

missed.claim: A canonical, torsor-level (functorial, sign-free) treatment of orientations in pseudoline arrangements, starting from the 3-line case. It is a stylistic contrast with the oriented-matroid literature, which uses chosen sign vectors and chirotopes. The content of this page itself is elementary and known.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is only potentially interesting if later pages build a functorial (choice-free) theory of oriented matroids or pseudoline systems from such torsor identities. On this page alone it is routine.

deep.surprise_reason: The page carefully but routinely sets up the cube/octahedron versus hemicube/hemi-octahedron correspondence and expresses orientations as contracted products of Z/2-torsors. All facts are classical; only the canonical-isomorphism style is characteristically Grothendieckian.
transcription_corrections: In diagram (5), the replacement for the crossed-out 'projectifs' in the right column is uncertain. Given the previous page systematically replaces 'projectif' by 'grand', it may read 'grands' rather than 'simpliciaux'.
'antiségments[?]' is uncertain. Mathematically the phrase refers to the two edges (segments) of D_i, i.e. elements of A_i = Φ_j ∧ Φ_k.

In (7), the parenthetical should read as 'un des deux côtés [edges] de Õ portés par D_i' rather than 'partagés'. A_i parametrizes the two edges lying on D_i, consistent with the previous page's description of lines via edges.
